definition.summary: Cystitis refers to inflammation or infection of the lower urinary tract, specifically the urinary bladder. It is derived from the Greek word 'kystis' meaning bladder.

types.uncomplicated: A lower UTI in a non-pregnant, premenopausal, otherwise healthy woman with no known urologic abnormalities or comorbidities.
types.complicated: A UTI associated with risk factors that increase the likelihood of complications, virulence of infection, or chances of antibiotic treatment failure.
types.acute: Characterized by sudden onset of symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort). Typically uncomplicated and responds well to antimicrobial therapy.
types.chronic: Persistent or recurrent inflammation of the bladder lining, often requiring more in-depth investigation into underlying causes.
types.hemorrhagic: Characterized by blood in the urine; can occur in both infectious and non-infectious forms.
types.radiation: A non-infectious form induced by radiation exposure, often as part of cancer treatment.
types.interstitial: A chronic, painful non-infectious form with unclear etiology, characterized by bladder wall inflammation.
types.catheter_associated: UTI occurring in patients with indwelling urinary catheters with signs and symptoms of infection and no other source.

epidemiology.general: UTIs are the most common bacterial infections in women, accounting for 8.6 million ambulatory care visits annually in the US.
epidemiology.women_lifetime_risk: Approximately 50% of women will experience at least one UTI in their lifetime.
epidemiology.annual_incidence_women: About 10% of women in the US have one or more symptomatic UTIs each year; estimated 0.5 to 0.7 UTIs per person-year in sexually active women.
epidemiology.age_group: Young, sexually active women aged 18-24 have the highest incidence.
epidemiology.spontaneous_resolution: About 25% of women have spontaneous resolution of symptoms.
epidemiology.men: Incidence in men is fewer than 10 cases per 10,000 men under age 65 per year; increases with age.
epidemiology.economic_burden: Approximately $1.6 billion in costs associated with acute uncomplicated cystitis in the US; $2 billion annually for ED UTI visits.
epidemiology.quality_of_life: Nearly half of affected women miss work or school; up to half avoid sexual activity for an average of one week.
epidemiology.recurrence: 25% of women experience recurrent cystitis within 6 months after their first UTI.

etiology_and_pathogens.most_common_pathogen: Escherichia coli (E. coli) causes 75-95% of uncomplicated UTIs.

uncomplicated_uti_pathogens.notes: Most common; uropathogenic strains use type 1 and P-fimbriae to adhere to uroepithelial cells.
Common in young sexually active women.
Second most common after E. coli; can form biofilms.
Produces urease; associated with complicated UTIs and stone formation.

complicated_uti_pathogens: Candida spp. (especially in catheterized patients on antibiotics)
etiology_and_pathogens.resistance_concern: E. coli resistance to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was 22.2% in 2012; resistance to ciprofloxacin was 11.8%; resistance to nitrofurantoin was only 0.9%. ESBL-producing E. coli is an increasing concern in community-acquired UTIs.

premenopausal_women: History of UTI or childhood UTI
Family history of UTI in first-degree female relative
complicated_uti_risk_factors: Renal disease or impaired renal function
Urinary tract abnormalities (vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, neurogenic bladder, stones)
Foreign bodies (urinary catheter, stent, nephrostomy tube)
Recent antibiotic use (within 3 months) — increases MDR risk
Recent hospitalization or long-term care facility residence
risk_factors.recurrent_uti_definition: Two or more UTIs within 6 months, OR three or more UTIs within 12 months.
risk_factors.men_uti: All UTIs in men are generally considered complicated until proven otherwise; evaluate for structural/functional abnormalities.

pathophysiology.mechanism: UTIs typically begin with periurethral contamination by a uropathogen from the gut/vaginal flora, followed by colonization of the urethra, then ascending migration to the bladder (or kidneys). Bacterial adherence to uroepithelium is the key pathogenic step.
pathophysiology.why_women_more_susceptible: Shorter urethra, proximity of urethral meatus to the anus, and moist periurethral environment facilitate bacterial ascent.
pathophysiology.virulence_factors: E. coli uses type 1 and P-fimbriae (adhesins) to bind uroepithelial receptors. Biofilm formation resists host defenses and antibiotics.
pathophysiology.pyelonephritis_mechanism: Uropathogens ascend to the kidneys via the ureters. Hematogenous spread is rare (mainly S. aureus).
pathophysiology.complicated_host_factors: Diabetes impairs immune response; renal insufficiency reduces host defenses; urinary stasis (from stones, obstruction) creates infection nidus; catheter biofilms harbor pathogens.

differentiating_uncomplicated_from_pyelo.cystitis_only: Lower urinary symptoms without systemic signs

clinical_presentation.high_predictive_value: New onset of frequency and dysuria with absence of vaginal discharge has a positive predictive value of 90% for UTI.

atypical_presentations.elderly: Confusion, behavioral changes, functional decline; classic urinary symptoms may be absent.
atypical_presentations.frail_debilitated: Changes in mental/functional status; only acute dysuria and urinary changes (gross hematuria, color/odor changes) reliably correlate with documented UTI.

clinical_presentation.notes: Urine cloudiness or odor alone in the absence of other symptoms is generally insufficient to justify a diagnosis of cystitis.

differential_diagnosis.differentiating_features: Vaginal discharge, vulvovaginal itch/soreness, odor, dyspareunia; typically no urinary urgency or frequency
Pyuria without bacteriuria; risk factors for STI; abnormal discharge
Fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea/vomiting
No evidence of infection (negative cultures); chronic pelvic/bladder pain; diagnosis of exclusion
Pelvic/lower abdominal pain, fever, cervical discharge, dyspareunia
Hematuria, interrupted urine flow, lower abdominal pain
Pelvic/perineal pain, fever, malaise, soft tender prostate on exam
Post-menopausal women; vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, thin watery discharge
Pain worsens with movement, nausea/vomiting, fever, bowel changes

clinical_diagnosis.summary: In young, non-pregnant women with typical symptoms (dysuria + frequency) and no vaginal discharge, clinical diagnosis alone may be sufficient to initiate treatment.
clinical_diagnosis.key_rule: Combination of dysuria and urinary frequency in the absence of vaginal discharge or irritation is 90% predictive of UTI.

key_findings: Leukocyte esterase (enzyme from WBCs — indicates pyuria)
Nitrites (indicates presence of Enterobacteriaceae; organisms convert nitrate to nitrite)
urinalysis.notes: Dipstick is cost-effective. Nitrites + leukocyte esterase together have 85% positive predictive value and 92% negative predictive value. Absence of pyuria suggests alternative diagnosis. Only Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Enterococcus fail to convert nitrates to nitrites.
urinalysis.specimen: Clean-catch midstream urine. No significant difference between cleansed and uncleansed specimens in contamination rates.

urine_culture.routine_uncomplicated: NOT routinely recommended for uncomplicated cystitis.
when_indicated: Symptoms not resolving or recurring within 2-4 weeks after treatment
Patients with risk factors for complicated UTI
urine_culture.colony_count: ≥ 100,000 CFU/mL = clinically relevant bacteriuria; ≥ 1,000 CFU/mL significant in men or straight catheter specimens; even 10-100 CFU/mL of E. coli in symptomatic women may be significant.

imaging.when: Patients not responding after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics; suspected obstruction, abscess, or stones.
imaging.modalities: CT scan (preferred, most sensitive); renal ultrasound + KUB (for radiation-sensitive patients).

diagnosis.pregnancy_test: Should be performed in women of childbearing age.

treatment.goals: Symptom relief, eradication of bacteriuria, prevention of progression to pyelonephritis or sepsis. Clinical response expected within 24 hours (cystitis) or 48-72 hours (pyelonephritis). Prefer narrow-spectrum agents with low collateral damage potential.

first_line_agents.notes: Preferred first choice. High cure rate (79-92%). Does NOT cause collateral damage. Avoid if CrCl < 30-60 mL/min (per different guidelines), if pyelonephritis suspected, or in urine pH ≥ 8. Avoid in first trimester and near-term pregnancy.

first_line_agents.dose: 160/800 mg (1 double-strength tablet) orally twice daily
first_line_agents.notes: Use only if local E. coli resistance < 20%. Cure rate 90-100%. Avoid if used in preceding 3 months, if sulfa allergy, or if resistance rate known to exceed 20%. Avoid in first trimester and after 32 weeks of pregnancy.

first_line_agents.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily (or 300 mg once nightly in Australian guidelines)
first_line_agents.notes: Alternative to TMP-SMX in sulfa-allergic patients. Similar efficacy.

first_line_agents.dose: 3 g orally as a single dose
first_line_agents.notes: Convenient single-dose regimen. Lower effectiveness than some agents. Broad spectrum including ESBL producers and Enterococcus (including VRE). Less effective against Klebsiella and Pseudomonas. FDA category B in pregnancy. Avoid if pyelonephritis suspected. Increasing resistance with increased use.
first_line_agents.resistance: Generally low, but rising with overuse.

second_line_agents.notes: Reserve for when first-line agents cannot be used. Risk of collateral damage (MDR organism selection). FDA safety communication: serious adverse events (tendinitis, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects) outweigh benefits for uncomplicated cystitis when alternatives are available.

second_line_agents.dose: 200 mg orally twice daily OR 400 mg single dose

alternative_agents_beta_lactams.notes: Use only when other agents cannot be used. Lower efficacy than TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolones. Clinical efficacy ~89% for oral beta-lactams used 3-5 days.
Widely used in practice but limited data; not recommended by IDSA for uncomplicated UTI but acceptable in some settings.

outpatient_first_line.dose: 500 mg orally twice daily OR 1g ER once daily

acute_uncomplicated_pyelonephritis.if_fq_resistance_over_10: Give initial dose of ceftriaxone 1g IV or consolidated aminoglycoside (gentamicin 5-7 mg/kg once), then transition to oral based on culture.
acute_uncomplicated_pyelonephritis.notes: Complete course with oral antibiotics after afebrile for 48 hours. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are NOT appropriate for pyelonephritis (poor renal tissue penetration).

complicated_cystitis.duration: 5-7 days for acute complicated cystitis; 7-14 days for complicated pyelonephritis
complicated_cystitis.esbl_producing_organisms: Nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin are oral options; parenteral ertapenem or piperacillin/tazobactam for severe cases.
complicated_cystitis.mdr_organisms: Colistin or tigecycline may be necessary; ceftolozane/tazobactam or ceftazidime/avibactam for MDR P. aeruginosa or non-NDM CRE.
complicated_cystitis.men: Treat as complicated UTI for minimum 7 days; fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX preferred; rule out prostatitis.

management: Remove and replace catheter before/when starting antibiotics if catheter in place ≥ 7 days
Obtain urine culture from newly placed catheter
Treat similarly to acute complicated cystitis
catheter_associated_uti.duration: 7 days if timely symptom resolution; 10-14 days if delayed response or bacteremia/severe sepsis
catheter_associated_uti.women_under_65_no_pyelonephritis: May treat for 3 days after catheter removal

safe_antibiotics.notes: Avoid first trimester (organogenesis) and near term (38-42 weeks; risk of neonatal hemolytic anemia)

avoid: TMP-SMX in first trimester (folate-sensitive birth defects)
uti_in_pregnancy.asymptomatic_bacteriuria: Screen all pregnant women at 12-16 weeks gestation; treat if positive to prevent pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
uti_in_pregnancy.pyelonephritis: Parenteral antibiotics for 48 hours before transitioning to oral therapy.

acute_bacterial.initial: Parenteral: ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q24h, ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h, or levofloxacin 500mg IV q24h

chronic_bacterial.first_line: Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID or levofloxacin 500mg daily for 4-6 weeks
chronic_bacterial.alternative: Trimethoprim 100mg BID for 4-12 weeks (good prostate penetration)
chronic_bacterial.adjuncts: Alpha-adrenergic antagonists (tamsulosin, alfuzosin) to reduce symptoms

non_antibiotic_strategies.evidence: Significantly reduces recurrent UTI risk; recurrence rates 14.6% vs 60.8% (no prophylaxis)

non_antibiotic_strategies.notes: Converted to formaldehyde in acidic urine; contraindicated if CrCl < 10 mL/min
Normalizes vaginal flora; 0.5mg estriol cream at night x2 weeks then twice weekly x8 months significantly reduces UTI incidence
Promising; L. rhamnosus GR-1 and L. reuteri RC-14 shown to reduce UTI in postmenopausal women
Blocks P-fimbriae adhesion; meta-analysis of 24 studies showed NO significant reduction in symptomatic UTIs. Not recommended for treatment. Possibly helpful as prophylaxis capsules in pregnancy.

behavioral_modifications: Increase fluid intake to 2-3 L daily
Double voiding to empty bladder completely

screen_and_treat: Prior to invasive urologic procedures / transurethral resection of prostate

symptomatic_relief.analgesics: Paracetamol or NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for pain and discomfort
symptomatic_relief.phenazopyridine: Urinary analgesic for short-term dysuria relief; NOT therapeutic; will not affect infection course
symptomatic_relief.urinary_alkalinizers: May relieve dysuria; unproven efficacy; contraindicated with nitrofurantoin, in renal failure, hypernatremia

principles: Select antibiotics based on UTI type, severity, and local susceptibility patterns
Use narrow-spectrum agents with low collateral damage potential for uncomplicated UTIs
Avoid routine screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria
Short courses are effective for uncomplicated cystitis
Consider analgesics (ibuprofen) as initial symptomatic treatment in uncomplicated UTIs before antibiotics
Avoid fluoroquinolones as first-line for uncomplicated cystitis (preserve for more serious infections)
Consider collateral damage: broad-spectrum cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones select for resistant organisms
antibiotic_stewardship.collateral_damage_concept: Ecological adverse effects of antibiotic therapy — selection of drug-resistant organisms, proliferation of MDR bacteria. Broad-spectrum cephalosporins linked to VRE, ESBL-producing Klebsiella, and C. difficile. Fluoroquinolones linked to MRSA and fluoroquinolone-resistant Pseudomonas.
mdr_risk_factors: Previous MDR isolate (resistant to ≥ 3 antibiotic classes)
Use of broad-spectrum antibiotics within preceding 3 months
TMP-SMX use within preceding 3-6 months (increases TMP-SMX resistance)

elderly.risk_factors: Faecal impaction, incontinence, vaginal/perineal atrophy, impaired bladder emptying, comorbidities, catheters, polypharmacy
elderly.presentation: May be typical or atypical (confusion, behavioral changes); cognitive impairment complicates assessment
elderly.recommendation: Refer patients > 65 years to physician for further evaluation; avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria
elderly.nitrofurantoin_note: Appropriate in elderly if CrCl ≥ 30 mL/min (2015 Beers Criteria update)

children.signs: Variable and often non-specific; urine sample required for diagnosis

renal_transplant_recipients.note: UTIs are the most common infectious complication post-transplant; occur in ~25% within 1 year; increase transplant failure/rejection risk 2-3 fold
renal_transplant_recipients.prophylaxis: TMP-SMX prophylaxis for 6 months (primarily for Pneumocystis jiroveci also prevents UTIs)

safe: Nitrofurantoin (avoid if infant < 1 month or G6PD deficient)
lactating_women.consult: LactMed for current data on individual antibiotics

skilled_nursing_facility.asb_prevalence: 15-50% of older adults in SNFs have ASB
skilled_nursing_facility.warning: ~50% of asymptomatic SNF residents are inappropriately given broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected UTI; ~80% of antibiotic use was based on urinalysis results alone without symptoms
skilled_nursing_facility.recommendation: Routine screening for ASB NOT recommended in SNF residents; treat only symptomatic patients

complications: Emphysematous cystitis (rare; gas in bladder wall; 2/3 have diabetes; ~10% require surgery)

immediate_referral: Signs of pyelonephritis: fever > 38°C, chills/rigors, flank pain, nausea/vomiting
Symptoms persist 48-72 hours after starting appropriate antibiotic
Symptoms recur within 2 weeks after completing treatment
Only one primary symptom of acute cystitis
Risk factors for complicated UTI (see risk factors section)
Recurrent UTI (≥ 2 within 6 months or ≥ 3 within 12 months)
Risk factors for sexually transmissible infection
Male patients (UTI in men generally complicated)

key_messages: Take the full antibiotic course even if symptoms improve early
Symptoms should improve within 24-48 hours of starting antibiotics
Void after sexual intercourse to flush bacteria
Wipe from front to back after using the toilet
Use condoms to reduce STI risk
Double voiding to empty bladder completely
Return to clinician if symptoms worsen, do not improve within 48 hours, or recur within 2 weeks

faq.question: What is cystitis?
faq.answer: Cystitis is inflammation of the urinary bladder, usually caused by a bacterial infection. It is the most common type of urinary tract infection (UTI), particularly in women. Key symptoms include burning or painful urination (dysuria), frequent urination, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort.

faq.question: What causes cystitis?
faq.answer: The most common cause is Escherichia coli (E. coli), responsible for 75-95% of cases. Other bacteria include Staphylococcus saprophyticus (especially in young women), Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis. Non-infectious causes include chemical irritants, radiation, and autoimmune reactions.

faq.question: Who is most at risk for cystitis?
faq.answer: Women are at much higher risk than men due to shorter urethra and proximity to the anus. Risk is highest in sexually active women aged 18-24. Other risk factors include sexual intercourse, spermicide use, pregnancy, diabetes, urinary tract abnormalities, catheter use, and immunosuppression.

faq.question: How is cystitis diagnosed?
faq.answer: In young healthy women with typical symptoms (dysuria + frequency) and no vaginal discharge, clinical diagnosis is highly accurate (90% positive predictive value). Urine dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrites supports the diagnosis. Urine culture is NOT routinely required for uncomplicated cystitis but is recommended for suspected pyelonephritis, treatment failure, recurrence, or complicated cases.

faq.question: What are the best antibiotics for uncomplicated cystitis?
faq.answer: First-line options are: (1) Nitrofurantoin 100mg twice daily for 5 days — preferred choice with very low resistance; (2) Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800mg twice daily for 3 days — if local resistance < 20%; (3) Fosfomycin 3g single dose — convenient but slightly less effective. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) are reserved as second-line due to risk of serious side effects and resistance.

faq.question: How long does cystitis treatment take?
faq.answer: Nitrofurantoin: 5 days; TMP-SMX: 3 days; Fosfomycin: single dose; Fluoroquinolones: 3 days; Beta-lactams: 5-7 days. Complicated UTIs require 10-14 days. Symptoms typically improve within 24-48 hours of starting treatment.

faq.question: Can cystitis go away without antibiotics?
faq.answer: Studies show 25-42% of women with uncomplicated cystitis achieve clinical cure without antibiotic treatment. Initial symptomatic treatment with ibuprofen may be considered in mild uncomplicated UTIs. However, antibiotics remain recommended to shorten symptom duration, prevent recurrence, and reduce progression to pyelonephritis.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor urgently?
faq.answer: Seek urgent medical attention if you have: fever > 38°C, chills or rigors, back or flank pain, nausea or vomiting (these suggest kidney infection/pyelonephritis), symptoms not improving after 48-72 hours of antibiotics, symptoms recurring within 2 weeks of completing treatment, or if you are pregnant.

faq.question: What is the difference between cystitis and pyelonephritis?
faq.answer: Cystitis (lower UTI) involves the bladder: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain — WITHOUT fever or systemic symptoms. Pyelonephritis (upper UTI) involves the kidneys: fever > 38°C, chills, flank/costovertebral angle pain, nausea/vomiting — often WITH lower UTI symptoms. Pyelonephritis is more serious and requires different (often longer) treatment.

faq.question: How can I prevent recurrent UTIs?
faq.answer: Key prevention strategies: void after sexual intercourse, increase fluid intake (2-3L/day), wipe front to back, avoid spermicides. Evidence-based options include D-mannose 2g daily, topical estrogen (postmenopausal women), Lactobacillus probiotics, and methenamine hippurate. Prophylactic antibiotics (low-dose nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX) are a last resort. Cranberry products show limited evidence.

faq.question: Is cystitis treatment different in pregnancy?
faq.answer: Yes. Pregnant women must be treated to prevent progression to pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Safe antibiotics include: nitrofurantoin (avoid first trimester and near term), amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, cephalexin, cefpodoxime, and fosfomycin. Avoid fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX in first trimester and after 32 weeks, and tetracyclines. Pregnant women should also be screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria.

faq.question: Can men get cystitis?
faq.answer: Yes, but it is much less common (fewer than 10 cases per 10,000 men under 65 per year). UTIs in men are always considered complicated until proven otherwise, requiring evaluation for structural/functional abnormalities and prostatitis. Treatment duration is typically 7-14 days.

faq.question: Why are fluoroquinolones not recommended first-line for cystitis?
faq.answer: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) are effective but are reserved for more serious infections because: (1) they can cause serious side effects (tendinitis, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects); (2) widespread use increases fluoroquinolone resistance; (3) they cause 'collateral damage' — selecting for resistant organisms like MRSA and MDR Pseudomonas in the gut flora. The FDA issued a safety communication in 2016 advising against routine use for uncomplicated cystitis.

faq.question: What is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)?
faq.answer: ASB is the presence of bacteria in urine (≥ 100,000 CFU/mL) without symptoms. It does NOT require treatment in most cases — including non-pregnant adults, elderly, diabetics, and catheterized patients. Treatment IS recommended only for pregnant women, those undergoing invasive urologic procedures, and renal transplant recipients (controversial). Treating ASB unnecessarily leads to antibiotic resistance and side effects.

faq.question: Does cranberry juice cure or prevent UTIs?
faq.answer: No. Cranberry inhibits bacterial P-fimbriae adhesion, which is theoretically beneficial. However, a meta-analysis of 24 studies (4,473 participants) showed cranberry products did NOT significantly reduce symptomatic UTIs. They are not recommended for treating an active UTI. Cranberry capsules may be an option for UTI prevention in pregnancy.

faq.question: What is a complicated UTI?
faq.answer: A complicated UTI occurs in patients with factors that increase infection risk, severity, or likelihood of treatment failure: pregnancy, men, urinary tract obstruction, immunosuppression, renal failure, renal transplantation, neurogenic bladder, indwelling catheters, anatomical abnormalities, diabetes (poorly controlled), or hospital-acquired infection. These require longer treatment (10-14 days) and broader antibiotic coverage.
